posts.name: Chaosmancer
posts.cooked:
Jeysie:

Based on some reactions in other convos here as of later, I think I'm going to stick by my feeling that anyone who likes whimsical or quirky or corny ideas sometimes isn't very welcome or is going to just get dead seriousness in response, so my roleplaying thoughts probably aren't terribly relevant.

 

For me, it's a knee jerk reaction.

 

I've had players (both as a DM and playing alongside me) who are "whimsical" in that [actual play example] they decide they are bored at the party of the most powerful wizard in the world, where we are acting as representatives of a respected merchant company, and then dump a plate of spaghetti on their head and wear it like a wig. All so they would be the center of attention.

 

Or, people who are "quirky" in that they murder civilians for being too ugly and steal their stuff, or threaten people with "humorous" tortures to make sure they aren't lying to the party about the fact that they are a merchant and don't know anything about the mysterious dungeon that just appeared outside of town.

 

Yeah, I've played with some people who are warped in some… interesting… ways. Not that most of them are that bad, not even a quarter most likely, but it's just a background noise for all of my games that I struggle with.

 

Now, your character you mention that loved machines and wanted to save the machines from the AI without damaging them is really cool, I love that sort of thing. But, I still yearn for a game where I can say the players aren't despicable people and they actually care about human lives and suffering, because I don't think I've had a group where every player was on that same page.

 

So, I want a "serious game" not in that I want grim and gritty, but a game where the players are the good guys, they are occasionally placed in situations where their morals and preconceptions can be challenged, and they struggle to remain good people who try to do the right thing, instead of deciding to cause massive destruction for little to no reason.

 

Also, I have a very dry sense of humor, and I tend towards being more serious. I couldn't play a character like your machine talking character, but that doesn't mean I'm not going to have fun interacting with you or that I won't have my own moments.

posts.name: Jeysie
posts.cooked:
See, I wouldn't want to play with characters like the ones you mentioned either, because they're just being Chaotic Stupid and OOC. That's bad roleplaying to me!

That's why it's so hard describing this stuff; people always jump to that sort of thing when it's like no, I agree that's just plain annoying. The idea isn't to derail a plot or be randomly stupid, it's to come up with characters with lots of interesting personality roleplaying hooks to build from and then seriously roleplay them.

I've played a variety of different characters depending on the campaign; some were more typically wholly good. (Though my techie wasn't anti-social, per se, she just liked machines better.) Another fave was a gnome inventor with a sunny and curious-about-everything personality who invented a sort of medieval MRE that we were delivering to a disaster-wrought town.

Like I said, think Setback or Unity for the types of characters that would show up in our games.

Oddly I'm also very serious and have a dry sense of humor, but--I guess this is more personal psychology than RPing--because I tend to be very logical and straightforward I tend to be drawn to/intrigued by things that are weird, creepy, whimsical, quirky, and/or creative. Things that challenge my perceptions, or challenge me to think and react in ways I normally wouldn't.

(I think that's why I like listening to and performing music so much as well; as Christopher said in the podcast, music is a strange mix of both art and logic/science.)

It was fun trying to think how my techie would react to that situation because she had an obviously unusual POV. With my gnome it was fun trying to think of how someone optimistic and bouncy would react to things when I'm usually pessimistic and restrained. I once played a fighter who was very much a combo of Blood Knight and The Ladette when I'm totally not either of those things.

It's more the difference between Legacy and Setback as characters. They're both very nice and good-aligned characters, but quite different in actual implementation.

posts.name: PlatinumWarlock
posts.cooked:
Chaosmancer:

For me, it's a knee jerk reaction. I've had players (both as a DM and playing alongside me) who are "whimsical" in that [actual play example] they decide they are bored at the party of the most powerful wizard in the world, where we are acting as representatives of a respected merchant company, and then dump a plate of spaghetti on their head and wear it like a wig. All so they would be the center of attention. Or, people who are "quirky" in that they murder civilians for being too ugly and steal their stuff, or threaten people with "humorous" tortures to make sure they aren't lying to the party about the fact that they are a merchant and don't know anything about the mysterious dungeon that just appeared outside of town. Yeah, I've played with some people who are warped in some… interesting… ways. Not that most of them are that bad, not even a quarter most likely, but it's just a background noise for all of my games that I struggle with. 

See, this is a massive pet-peeve of mine as a GM: the player who decides to be wacky "in-character", because they themselves want amusement, or view themselves as the center of the attention because–due to the nature of the medium–they're among the primary protagonists.  Worse so, if they're masking this desire under "I'm only doing what my character would!"  In doing so, they're actively conveying the message that their fun is more important than the fun of anyone (perhaps everyone) else at the table; it's selfish, it's self-centered, and it's arrogant.

I'm a big believer in consequence in my games.  You do something dumb, the in-game hammer's going to come down.  If you want to wear a bowl of spaghetti at the grand duchess's ball, you're going to be 1) shunned by pretty much every noble there, 2) escorted out of the ball by force, and 3) pretty well ignored by me for the remainder of the session.  As a GM, I'm not going to incentivize that sort of behavior by giving that player a "solo adventure" because they didn't feel like acting in a setting-appropriate manner.

For the character that's goes on a killing spree or actively threatening people, the same thing applies.  Killing a sentient being–even in a generic fantasy setting like D&D, where killing orcs and goblins is a given–is a big deal.  If there are witnesses, you can bet your bottom dollar that the police/town-guard/etc. will be knocking on their door.  Assets will be seized, trials will be held, and prison time is a reality.  Again, as GM, you shouldn't incentivize the behavior or sentiment that "I was bored, so I made my own amusement by wrecking your setting."

Now, for me, the way you convey this has to be directly.  If someone wants to take a questionable action, the GM has to hold the authority to say, "If you do that, XXXX is going to happen.  If that's what you want, that's fine; just don't be surprised by the consequences."  I'd say that, in my experience, 90+% of the time, that gets a player to reconsider.  For the ~10% of the times it doesn't, the player's been explicitly warned and you're in the clear to bring down the headsman's axe.

posts.name: Jeysie
posts.cooked:
Yeah, I was going to say to TakeWalker: The problem with Chaosmancer's post is more that the players in question were using their roleplaying power to be disruptive and annoying to the other players and their PC.

I have both played in games where chaotic and random things happening was a central plot/RPing point, and games where the PCs all had dodgy morals, but it was situations where we all agreed ahead of time that we were going to do these things and that we'd react realistically to any disruptions that occurred and the GM was OK with it and it fit the rules of the GM's story and so on and so on.

But if you instead have it where there's a character who goes off and does chaotically disruptive things when the other players are trying to seriously solve a plot, or a character doing dodgy or downright evil things in a group of otherwise good characters who are supposed to be doing good things, it's just plain old bad and annoying.

With great roleplaying power comes great responsibility.

Forgot to add that the reason I liked your Virtuoso plot idea you mentioned in another thread was because of the interesting juxtapositions between an as-yet-unaddressed consequence of the canon plot, someone who has every right to be angry, and them being angry at someone who had zero intention to do what they did and almost certainly wouldn't have had they known what would happen. It's an interesting tangle that's not at all straightforward.

And therein lies the roleplaying opportunity for me.  In a perfect world, Xu's spirit would be helping Anthony teach the future Virtuosos in the ways of music and the Void.  But, because he made a stupid decision–ignorant might be a better word than stupid here; he wasn't aware that destroying the Bell would have the consequences it would, even though doing so is inherently selfish and destructive–Xu has a right to feel angry, particularly given her fate (at least, in my mind, as a villain).  Argent Adept can be as sorry as he likes, but it's not going to bring the bell back, and it's not going to bring Xu's spirit back.  And, if you're his student, it's a legacy that you'll have to deal with…

posts.name: Jeysie
posts.cooked:
Which kind of ties into why I like roleplaying more "ordinary" or quirky characters. Argent is definitely in the "normal guy who gets saddled with powers and reacts to them in normal person ways" category of things and does a lot of "well, it seemed like a good idea at the time..." sort of things as a result that lead to interesting consequences when they're not actually good ideas.

Contrast, say, Legacy, who was literally born to do this stuff. He's more of the Standard Heroic Character people seem to usually play; he always knows what's the right thing to do and what isn't, he's always on top of things, he doesn't have many notable personality flaws. And thus not the sort of character I really know what to do with even though that's the sort of character most RPG folks seem to like to play.

posts.name: Rabit
posts.cooked:
Comrade Bubbles:

As an aside, I think it was Mike Mearls of the D&D team who recommends that your prep time takes no longer than the session length. Obviously, some things will take longer than others to prep, but that does seem to be the sweet spot, in my experience anyway.

Prep time is always an interesting topic.   (Yes, I've been wanting to respond to this for more than a week. Sad, right?  )

We have a friend who preps very little, as she is amAZing at improv. I, on the other hand, need to "talk to" NPCs in my head for a long time before I get their voice set well enough I feel like I can actually roleplay them in a session. That means I have to spend a lot more time on prep than many GMs. I also tend to do things that are a little more complex in nature. I'm also generally not willing to run published adventures as-is (that's a longer post than I have time for tonight), so I spend a great deal of time not just getting to know the material, but also customizing it for my own use. 

These are not normal things. They are things I've learned over the years. Most GMs will do just fine (and are probably better off!) using published materials for their first few games. That gives them an easy starting point and a basis upon which they can learn the craft. Once they get comfortable with GMing, they can branch out, experiment, etc.

Using what GtG is providing in the Sentinels RPG Starter Kit will be great for starting GMs! Read it, get to know it, get the "voice"/personality for the NPCs (especially the villains) in your head, make sure the players are playing one of the characters that fits their personal play style, and you'll do great.

posts.name: Comrade Bubbles
posts.cooked:
Rabit:

Prep time is always an interesting topic.   (Yes, I've been wanting to respond to this for more than a week. Sad, right?  )

We have a friend who preps very little, as she is amAZing at improv.

Not sad at all! Gods know I take my time replying to things sometimes.

I must admit, a lot of my prep time is just looking over notes to refresh myself on character names, place names and the like (the joys of homebrew). I usually figure out what story beats I'd like to happen during the week and then figure out how to make them as applicable as possible depending on what the players decide to do. Obviously there is some guiding happening during the game, but I like to improv that so its more fluid and reactive to the player's wishes.

But for new GMs, don't expect to be good at improv right of the bat. This is something I've taught myself to do and it really works FOR ME. I've found that if I over prepare; 1) most of it goes unused/recycled and 2) my anxiety kicks in about making sure everything fits perfectly together.
